query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor silicon content (~1–2 atomic %) to refractory high-entropy alloys will promote the in-situ formation of silicide phases and a continuous protective silica (SiO2) scale during extended high-temperature exposure in air, thereby significantly enhancing the alloy's oxygen resistance relative to the untreated material.
generation.material_initial_state: A typical refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., based on tungsten, molybdenum, tantalum, niobium, and vanadium) produced under standard processing conditions without silicon additions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor silicon addition (~1–2 at.%) into the alloy composition during fabrication.
generation.conditions: Heat treatment in an air atmosphere at approximately 1200°C for 10 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: In-situ formed silicide particles which, upon oxidation, develop a continuous silica (SiO2) layer at the surface.
generation.mechanism: Silicon in the alloy oxidizes preferentially to form silicide phases that convert into a robust and adherent SiO2 scale at high temperatures, impeding oxygen ingress and slowing further oxidation of the underlying refractory phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: The silicon-modified RHEA is expected to exhibit reduced oxidation rates, evidenced by decreased oxide scale thickness and lower weight gain compared to the untreated alloy under identical high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys typically develop thicker oxide scales and higher oxidation-induced weight gains when exposed to high-temperature air.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect of silicon is predicted to be significant at extreme high-temperature conditions (around 1200°C in air) but may not manifest under lower temperatures or in non-oxidizing environments.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal silicon concentration and its influence on oxidation kinetics, scale adherence, and long-term mechanical integrity require further clarification, and interactions with other alloying elements may affect the overall performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of refractory high-entropy alloy samples: one set incorporating a minor silicon addition (~1–2 at.%) and one control set without silicon. Subject both sets to an oxidation test by heating in air at 1200°C for 10 hours. Employ scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and gravimetric analysis to compare oxide scale thickness and weight gain between the two sets.
measurements: Weight gain due to oxidation (gravimetric analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the silicon-modified samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxide scale thickness and weight gain compared to the untreated control samples under the specified conditions, then the hypothesis that silicon addition improves oxygen resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Performance and environmental targets for future aero-engines could be met with changes in the propulsive and thermal efficiency of the engines and new materials that have capabilities beyond those of Ni-based superalloys. Industry has set the following property goals for new ultra-high temperature alloys with capabilities beyond those of Ni-based superalloys: the room temperature fracture toughness must be above 20 MPa(m)1/2, there must be less than 1% creep in 125 h at 1473 K and σ > 170 MPa (alloy density ρ = 7 g/cm3) and the oxidation life at 1588 K must be equal to that of second generation single crystal Ni-based superalloys at 1423 K, with a short term oxidation goal to have sufficient oxidation resistance in the uncoated condition to survive under typical engine conditions, which requires a loss of material less than 200 μm thickness in 10 h at 1643 K and a long term oxidation goal that requires a loss of material less than 25 μm thickness in 100 h at 1588 K [].

Niobium silicide based alloys can offer a balance of low, intermediate, and high temperature properties and are candidate materials to replace Ni-based superalloys in future aero-engines, to enable the latter to meet environmental and performance targets []. The latter have been set by industry and are property goals for new ultra-high temperature alloys with capabilities beyond those of Ni-based superalloys: the room temperature fracture toughness must be above 20 MPa(m)1/2, there must be less than 1% creep in 125 h at 1200 °C and σ > 170 MPa (alloy density ρ = 7 g/cm3), and the oxidation life at 1315 °C must be equal to that of second generation single crystal Ni-based superalloys at 1150 °C with a short term oxidation goal to have sufficient oxidation resistance in the uncoated condition to survive under typical engine conditions, which requires a loss of material less than 200 µm thickness in 10 h at 1370 °C and a long term oxidation goal that requires a loss of material less than 25 µm thickness in 100 h at 1315 °C []. reading.lever: Introduce minor silicon additions to promote in-situ silicide formation that develops a protective silica scale at extreme temperatures.
reading.why: Leveraging silicon’s proven ability in Nb-silicide alloys to form robust protective oxide layers could directly counter high-temperature oxygen degradation in RHEAs.
